query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled fraction of a refractory element such as niobium (Nb) into a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will lead to the formation of fine, thermally stable, nano-precipitates that hinder dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby improving the alloy’s high-temperature yield and creep resistance compared to the Nb-free composition.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents (with each element in the range of 5–35 at%) forming a simple solid solution phase.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor addition (e.g., 5–10 at%) of niobium into the alloy composition while keeping all elements within the 5–35 at% compositional definition. After alloy synthesis, apply a tailored heat treatment to promote the formation of nano-precipitates.
generation.conditions: The alloy is tested at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1000 °C) relevant for high-temperature structural applications, and the overall composition must adhere to the high-entropy alloy definition (each element between 5 and 35 at%).
generation.structural_mediator: Fine, well-dispersed, Nb-rich nano-precipitates within the primarily titanium/nickel solid solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: Nb atoms, due to their refractory nature and solid-solution/precipitate strengthening effect, are expected to partition during the heat treatment to form stable nano-precipitates. These precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation movement (dislocation pinning) at high temperatures, which enhances the yield strength and creep resistance of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Nb-containing alloy will demonstrate a higher yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the alloy without Nb. Although exact improvement levels are uncertain, an anticipated strength increase on the order of a moderate percentage (tentatively ~15–30%) is expected if the mechanism is active.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without the Nb addition and without the same heat treatment procedure.
generation.boundary: The intervention is valid only when the refractory addition does not push the composition outside of the 5–35 at% range for each constituent and when the heat treatment parameters (temperature and time) are optimized to promote nano-precipitation without forming deleterious coarse phases. Testing must be conducted under specific elevated-temperature conditions (around 800–1000 °C) relevant for intended applications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in mechanical properties (e.g., percentage increase in yield strength) is uncertain and may vary depending on the precise Nb content, processing conditions, and testing temperature. Furthermore, the stability and distribution of the nano-precipitates must be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the titanium/nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without Nb and a second set with an Nb addition of 5–10 at%. Apply an identical tailored heat treatment to both sets designed to promote nano-precipitate formation in the Nb-added alloy. Subject both sets to mechanical testing at elevated temperatures (e.g., 900 °C) including tensile and creep tests to measure yield strength and creep rate.
measurements: Creep resistance (strain rate under constant stress)
Microstructural characterization (using TEM or SEM) to verify the presence, size, and distribution of nano-precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (beyond measurement uncertainty, e.g., less than a 5% increase) in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the baseline samples, or if nano-precipitates are not observed in the microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Refractory elements, including Rhenium (Re), Molybdenum (Mo), Niobium (Nb), Tantalum (Ta), and Tungsten (W) [] are very important for improving mechanical properties in advanced alloys such as Titanium alloys and Nickel-base superalloys. Generally, elements with a melting point higher than Titanium (Ti), such as Chromium (Cr), Hafnium (Hf), Osmium (Os), Ruthenium (Ru), Vanadium (V), and Zirconium (Zr) are also classified as refractory elements. In Titanium alloys, refractory elements, especially Mo and W, are all beta stabilizers and possess a strong solid solution strengthening characteristic []. Nb forms Ni3Nb γ phase in Nickel-base superalloys such as Inconel 718 []. The improved creep resistance of the sixth generation superalloy TMS-238 mainly results from Re and Ru additions []. Refractory alloys also play significant roles in industry. In the second generation nuclear power plants, the most-used materials for fuel cladding are Zircoloy 2 and Zircoloy 4. The Niobium alloy C103 is used for the nozzle extension of satellites [].
